title: Perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a phase 2 trial
desc: In a nonrandomized phase 2 trial, patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer received perioperative ivonescimab as monotherapy or with chemotherapy, leading to encouraging pathological response rates in both cohorts, and sustained circulating tumor DNA negativity throughout neoadjuvant therapy may be predictive of response. Resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carries a high risk of postoperative recurrence, underscoring the need for effective perioperative therapies. This nonrandomized, noncomparative phase 2 trial evaluated neoadjuvant ivonescimab monotherapy (cohort 1) or in combination with chemotherapy (cohort 2), followed by surgery and adjuvant ivonescimab. In cohort 2, the major pathological response (MPR) rate was 70.1% (47/67; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 57.7–80.7); the lower bound of the 80% two-sided CI exceeded the historical control rate of 41% and the primary endpoint was met. The MPR rate in cohort 1 was 60.0% (6/10; 95% CI = 26.2–87.8). Among patients who achieved MPR, 83.3% (5/6) in cohort 1 and 97.9% (46/47) in cohort 2 had residual viable tumor (RVT) of ≤5%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 36.4% (4/11) patients in cohort 1 and 30.4% (24/79) of those in cohort 2, with no grade 3 or higher hemorrhage or treatment-related death. Treatment-related surgery delay occurred in one (1.3%) patient. Surgery-related AEs related to ivonescimab occurred in 10.0% (1/10) and 10.4% (7/67) patients in the two cohorts, respectively, with no grade 3 or higher events reported. These data support perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy as a promising strategy for resectable NSCLC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05247684 .

title: External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Delirium Risk.
desc: [JAMA network open] Although external validation of machine learning (ML)-based delirium risk models is a key stage in the model development pipeline, few published reports exist. Moreover, ML-based delirium risk models commonly degrade in performance during external validation. To examine the performance of a fusion multimodal with natural language processing (NLP) delirium risk stratification model in live clinical practice with cross-hospital external validation. This quality improvement study evaluated live clinical deployment of the model among patients 60 years or older who were admitted to non-intensive care units at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), with external validation performed at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025. Primary outcomes were performance of the risk stratification model, assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and monthly delirium detection rates. A 2 × 2 confusion matrix was created, and the 4 cells were used to calculate model performance metrics and compare associated diagnostic yield between premodel deployment and active model deployment periods. The overall sample included 33 095 admissions to non-intensive care units at MSM and MSH (mean [SD] age, 74.86 (9.22) years; 15 601 women [47.1%], 17 271 men [52.2%]). A total of 9020 MSM inpatient admissions were assigned a delirium risk score by the risk stratification model during live clinical operations and were compared to 21 186 MSH inpatient admissions that were assigned a risk score by the same model. Age at admission significantly differed between patients at MSM and MSH (MSM: median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years vs MSH: 72.62 [66.64-79.65] years; P < .001). Patients from MSM and MSH also significantly differed by sex, race and ethnicity, surgical vs medical primary diagnosis, length of stay, and dementia prevalence rate. Among 11 909 MSM patients, patients in the pre-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 78.00 [71.00-85.00] years) were significantly older than those in the post-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years) (P < .001). The AUROC of the model was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.90-0.92) for MSM and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for MSH. The positive predictive value of the model was 25.9% for MSM and 19.4% for MSH. For MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate significantly increased from 9.23% (95% CI, 8.07%-10.38%) to 19.59% (95% CI, 17.32%-21.85%) after model deployment (P < .001). title: Cross-paradigm audit of large language model judges for clinical text evaluation
desc: Large language models are increasingly being used to evaluate clinical texts, a concept known as LLM-as-a-judge. However, most of the existing evidence focuses on English data and uses pooled agreement metrics that obscure clinically relevant failure modes. This study audited six open-weight models against expert judges on four German clinical datasets covering report and nursing documentation summarization, discharge summary generation, and patient letter generation. The models were evaluated across three paradigms and four prompt configurations. Alignment with experts varied by criterion and corpus, and no configuration proved reliable across paradigms. All judges exhibited position and identity bias. Substituting LLM-as-a-judge for the expert panel shifted 57.2% of pointwise categories, swapped 41.7% of pairwise winners, missed 10.2% of clinical errors, and inverted clinical priorities by overrating the criteria succinct and accurate. Therefore, LLM-as-a-judge is not a safe substitute for experts in German clinical text evaluations, and deployment thresholds should follow decision-impact analysis for LLM-as-a-judge in clinical contexts.

desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Tianjin Medical University Second Hospital; conditions: Digital Health, Artificial Intelligence (AI); type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 420; status: RECRUITING] This is a prospective, single-center, controlled real-world study in patients with advanced solid tumors (stage III-IV) receiving chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or endocrine therapy. Participants who choose the digital management group use a smartphone-based oncology management application with medication reminders, AI-assisted laboratory report interpretation, adverse event self-reporting, and clinician alerts for critical values. Participants who choose the conventional group receive routine outpatient follow-up and telephone contact without digital tools. The aim is to evaluate whether a digital whole-course management model improves medication safety, reduces healthcare burden, and supports treatment adherence in advanced cancer care.

title: A Primer on Radiomics for the Practicing Orthopaedic Surgeon.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Global research & reviews
desc: [Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Global research & reviews] Artificial intelligence (AI) is permeating many aspects of daily life. Medicine, and specifically orthopaedic surgery, is being influenced by the rapid growth and success of AI in serving as an adjunct to medical expertise. AI includes many nested subfields and applications such as computer vision, language models, and predictive analytics. Using standard machine learning methods, clinical decision support tools are being developed for clinicians to provide evidence-based, individualized care. Some models predict clinical and functional outcomes after a procedure, whereas others may incorporate administrative metrics to predict factors, such as length of stay, return to the emergency department, and complications. The application of AI to medical imaging focuses on the extraction of a large amount of quantitative data in the form of predefined features from clinical images that humans cannot perceive, a field known as radiomics. There has been recent interest, particularly in oncology, to apply radiomics to aid in diagnosis and prognostication of outcomes. Given the robust growth of radiomics literature, and the anticipated application in orthopaedic surgery, the purpose of this review article is to educate the orthopaedic surgery community on the practical importance and the basics of radiomics.

title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
desc: Progress in AI is often measured by what a single model can do on its own. Yet teams of AI agents are starting to make breakthroughs and discoveries in science, medicine, mathematics and software engineering. As AI begins to work in teams of agents and people, the ability to collaborate becomes a core part of their intelligence. Research on human teams has measured this ability for decades. Inspired by this, we introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate. It contains 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark, from aviation accident reports and clinical cases to coding tasks and negotiations, and has a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks that they can solve by themselves when they have full information. We evaluate 18 closed- and open-weight models and find that every model, across sizes and families, has clear weaknesses as a teammate, with the best model scoring only 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they cave under interpersonal pressure, reaching the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts, and their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Crucially, general capability does not guarantee good teamwork, as models with nearly the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The benchmark includes 160 public tasks with code and data, along with 80 held-out tasks for evaluation. As AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents and people, the ability to collaborate effectively is becoming a crucial capability to measure and develop.

title: Multimodal Fusion Methods for Whole-Slide Images and Clinical Data in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
desc: Multimodal AI fusion of histology and clinical data is an active research area in computational pathology, but fusion methods are rarely compared under identical conditions and across different clinical endpoints. We present a modular framework in which slide-level embeddings, obtained by training an attention-based aggregator over patch embeddings from a frozen foundation model, and per-visit clinical embeddings are fed into 15 interchangeable fusion methods with a shared output dimension and prediction head (except decision-level methods). Using a prospective cohort of newly diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease patients, we predicted STRIDE-II-aligned remission outcomes from baseline or follow-up visits. The best fusion method reached macro-F1 of 0.57-0.75, outperforming both single-modality models in four of six scenarios, and differed by outcome and input. Image reliance, the drop in balanced accuracy when the slide embedding is removed, tended to follow the remission type - highest for histological and lowest for endoscopic remission; methods with similar accuracy relied on the slide to very different degrees.

title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
desc: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920-0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875-0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672-0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

title: Evaluating uncertainty for detecting performance loss and guiding deferral after model transfer between hospital systems
desc: Clinical prediction models often perform worse after transfer between hospital systems, but deterioration becomes apparent only once outcomes are known. We investigated whether uncertainty measures available at prediction time warn of performance loss and can help identify individual predictions requiring review. Three neural network architectures were trained on MIMIC-IV for in-hospital mortality prediction and evaluated on eICU-CRD. Measures included predictive entropy, mutual information from Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles, and representation density. After transfer, AUROC fell from 0.86-0.87 to 0.76-0.77 and calibration worsened, while entropy and mutual information were lower. None of the measures reliably indicated the reduced performance. Deferring the 20% with the highest entropy reduced the remaining error rate from 17.5-20.1% to 6.3-8.0%; the deferred patients included 91-99% of false alarms but only 2-7% of missed deaths, which carried low uncertainty. Uncertainty therefore supported selective review but failed to reveal performance loss.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Maternal Health Outcomes in Pregnant and Postpartum Individuals: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
desc: [JAMA network open] Generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used to support maternal health, but randomized evidence is limited. To evaluate whether access to a generative AI maternal health chatbot improved 12-month maternal health outcomes. This 2-group randomized clinical trial enrolled 400 participants from October 2023 to December 2024, with 12-month follow-up completed in December 2025. Participants were recruited online across 49 US states and the District of Columbia. Eligible participants were English-speaking, aged 14 years or older, pregnant or parenting an infant younger than 6 months, and self-identified as members of racial and/or ethnic minoritized groups. Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive access to the chatbot or an active control consisting of monthly children's books. Primary outcomes were anxiety and depression symptoms at 12 months measured using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and Patient Health Questionnaire-9. Secondary outcomes included emergency department visits, pregnancy-related complications, postpartum care checkups, effective contraception use, and sleep duration. Among 400 randomized participants, the mean (SD) age was 32.6 (5.1) years; 200 (50%) were parenting an infant at enrollment; and 10 (2%) identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, 80 (20%) Asian, 188 (47%) Black or African American, 57 (14%) multiracial, and 65 (16%) Hispanic or Latino. The AI chatbot was not associated with differences in anxiety scores (adjusted mean difference, 0.10; 95% CI, -0.77 to 0.96) or depression scores (adjusted mean difference, -0.23; 95% CI, -1.05 to 0.59), nor with emergency department visits, postpartum care, contraception use, or sleep duration. Among participants pregnant at enrollment, the chatbot was associated with more self-reported pregnancy-related complications in the secondary 12-month end point analysis, but not in longitudinal analyses. Higher chatbot engagement was associated with longer sleep duration and higher anxiety scores in exploratory within-group analyses. In this randomized clinical trial of pregnant and postpartum individuals from racial and ethnic minoritized groups, access to a generative artificial intelligence maternal health chatbot did not improve maternal anxiety or depression at 12 months compared with an active control. Secondary and exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06053515.

title: A multimodal tool-augmented agent for evidence-based clinical decision support in longitudinal AMD follow-up
desc: Clinical management of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) requires longitudinal decisions on disease activity, treatment response, and anti-VEGF injection intervals. These decisions depend on integrating multimodal retinal imaging findings across visits, yet manual synthesis is time-consuming and may omit relevant information, limiting transparency and consistency in follow-up planning. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored to summarize longitudinal AMD information, but existing approaches may lack explicit quantitative grounding and evidence attribution, reducing their auditability in clinical decision support. To address these limitations, we developed AMDagent, an evidence-grounded clinical agent that integrates quantitative imaging analysis with guideline retrieval to generate structured, clinician-facing decision-support outputs. The system links longitudinal imaging findings to actionable management considerations while preserving traceable evidence sources. In a 20-case proof-of-concept evaluation of curated longitudinal AMD cases, AMDagent was rated clinically appropriate in 92.0% of predefined decision-support units under expert adjudication. In addition, 83.3% of audited major clinical claims were explicitly grounded in tool-derived quantitative measurements and/or retrieved guideline evidence, enabling clinician verification. These preliminary findings suggest that evidence-grounded, clinician-facing agents may support more transparent and auditable longitudinal AMD decision support, although larger prospective multi-center studies are needed to assess generalizability and clinical utility.

desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: China National Center for Cardiovascular Diseases; conditions: Hypertension, Hyperglycemia, Dyslipidemia; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 150; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] High blood pressure often occurs together with abnormal blood glucose, abnormal blood lipids, or abdominal obesity. Managing these conditions outside the hospital can be difficult. This study will test whether a digital health program that combines artificial intelligence (AI) with review and support by doctors and nurses improves health outcomes compared with standard out-of-hospital guidance. The study will enroll 150 adults aged 18 to 70 years who have hypertension and at least one additional cardiometabolic risk factor that is not at target. Participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the hybrid AI-assisted management group or the standard-guidance group. The intervention group will use a patient mini-program and connected devices to monitor blood pressure, glucose, and lifestyle information. The AI system will propose personalized medication, diet, exercise, and monitoring plans, which the healthcare team will review and confirm before delivery. The control group will receive routine printed health education and usual clinical follow-up. All participants will be followed for 6 months. The main outcome is the proportion of participants achieving blood pressure control together with control of at least one glycemic or lipid indicator. Other assessments include treatment adherence, cardiovascular events, hospitalizations, medical costs, quality of life, and system usability.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Assessment and Conservative Treatment of Lateral Epicondylosis.
desc: [Southern medical journal] Artificial intelligence (AI) is used increasingly to support clinical care and documentation in health care, including patient rehabilitation. AI is used to increase efficiency, facilitate information transfer, and improve accuracy and consistency in assessment and treatment of medical conditions. AI can assist clinicians in correlating symptoms, tracking patient progress, and recommending evidence-based treatment protocols. This article first provides perspectives on the role of AI in managing lateral epicondylosis. It then embarks on a preliminary study that compares expert opinions with AI recommendations for evaluation and treatment and provides insight into how patient expectations are influenced by AI searches in comparison to clinician recommendations. Although AI offers the potential of valuable support, clinicians remain responsible for final decisions to ensure optimal patient outcomes. The role of AI continues to evolve in clinical practice. It holds promise for advancing standards in the nonoperative management of lateral epicondylosis with the caveat that clinicians-human beings-have the ultimate responsibility and accountability for appropriate application and decision making to thoughtfully care for patients and improve treatment outcomes.

title: SphereFlow: Missing Modality Imputation via Geometric Transport on Hypersphere
desc: Missing modality imputation aims to synthesize unobserved modalities from observed ones. Existing methods treat each modality as living on its own latent manifold, forcing the generator to learn a long, unstructured jump between them. We present SphereFlow, which takes a fundamentally different view: by projecting all modalities into a shared hyperspherical latent space via a frozen self-supervised encoder, cross-modal imputation reduces to short-range geometric transport between nearby points on the sphere. Realizing this idea with flow matching, however, exposes two geometric conflicts: the standard Gaussian noise source is catastrophically mismatched with the unit-norm data manifold, and the linear interpolation path departs the sphere surface into a region where the decoder has no training signal. We resolve both with simple, geometry-aware modifications: replacing the noise source with the observed-modality latent so that the velocity field learns only the cross-modal displacement, and training the decoder with a time-weighted loss that extends its domain to the near-surface region traversed by the flow. We prove that this data-as-source formulation reduces the worst-case off-manifold deviation from a quantity that grows with the latent dimension to a small, dimension-independent bound governed by inter-modality similarity. Experiments on BraTS multi-modal MRI imputation and CT-MRI translation demonstrate state-of-the-art generation fidelity across all settings, while downstream brain tumor segmentation with our imputed data closes roughly eighty percent of the gap to the full-modality oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/WTHH031230/SphereFlow.

title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials
desc: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.

title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
desc: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

Global temperature-related mortality associated with El-Nino Southern Oscillation
desc: Epidemiological estimates suggest that global heat-related mortality increased by 29% during very strong El Niño years, with the greatest burdens occurring in low- and medium- Human Development Index regions. El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influences the global climate through interconnected atmospheric processes, yet its impact on global and regional temperature-related mortality burden remains unquantified. Here, we integrate global temperature and mortality databases with epidemiological models to assess temperature-related mortality associated with ENSO variability and intensity. During very strong El Niño years, the large amounts of heat released into the atmosphere are associated with an increase in global heat-related mortality of +28.87% (+107,035 annual deaths; 95% eCI: 27,336 to 176,312), and a decrease in global cold-related mortality of −3.70% (−112,681 annual deaths; 95% eCI: -207,619 to -22,203). Increase in heat-related mortality was concentrated in low and medium HDI countries, which accounted for 67.65% of the global increase, with the largest increase in medium HDI countries (+61,863 annual deaths; 95% eCI: 19,939 to 105,888), while point estimates of the combined heat and cold burden suggest a shift of the total burden from high toward lower HDI countries. In a context of continuously warming temperatures, our results indicate that forthcoming El Niño events have the potential to represent new public health challenges, underscoring the need for climate-informed preparedness actions.

title: A multi-guideline clinical agent for vascular surgery: architecture, implementation, and benchmark evaluation.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] The clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) published by the European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) span approximately 1100 pages whose simultaneous cross-referencing is impractical at the point of care. Unguarded large language models (LLMs) carry hallucination risk, motivating a guideline-locked design. We describe the architecture and development of a context-aware clinical agent encompassing the full ESVS corpus of 14 CPGs. The system extends a validated single-guideline GraphRAG prototype with an LLM-driven Guideline Router, an embedded Context Gate that withholds retrieval when decision-critical parameters are absent, dual-channel retrieval, and GPT-5 synthesis under a mandatory citation template. An automated benchmark assessed the final system on 55 vignettes, scored by 2 blinded LLM judges over 3 runs (330 judgments), with clinician adjudication of every flagged claim. The system stayed within its locked corpus, declined all out-of-scope queries, and achieved 98.4% guideline-routing recall. The Context Gate showed 91.9% specificity and 78.6% sensitivity for underspecified queries, and all 259 cited recommendations were verifiable within the locked corpus. Automated judges flagged an unsupported claim in 18.2% of items under a sensitive screening definition; on adjudication by 2 vascular surgeons, 7.3% of items contained a clinically consequential error, none graded capable of causing harm. Clinical acceptability of complete answers was not scored and is reserved for prospective expert evaluation. These results support the feasibility of a multi-guideline context-aware clinical agent for vascular surgery; citation traceability and locked-corpus provenance facilitate future auditability.

title: Digital and hybrid interventions for subacute and chronic low back pain: component network meta-analysis
desc: Digital and hybrid interventions combining exercise, education, and psychological components are increasingly used for low back pain (LBP), but it remains unclear which components and combinations drive efficacy. We conducted a prospectively registered component network meta-analysis (CNMA) to evaluate their efficacy and safety for non-specific LBP. Six databases and two trial registries were searched to May 2025. Data on disability, pain intensity, and adverse events were analysed using a Bayesian random-effects CNMA. Of 2809 records, 56 reports of 46 studies (6717 participants; 80% chronic low back pain) were included. Hybrid interventions combining digital and in-person exercise with in-person psychological components (MD: –22.21; 95%-CrI: –34.11 to –10.67), digital and in-person exercise (MD: –15.75; 95%-CrI: –22.79 to –8.80), or digital exercise with physiotherapy (MD: –13.17; 95%-CrI: –21.18 to –5.16) reduced disability versus no intervention at short-term (minimal clinically important difference (MCID): 4.92/100 Oswestry Disability Index). Digital and in-person exercise (MD: -1.76; 95%-CrI: -2.62; -0.87) and combined digital exercise training with in-person education (MD: -1.73; 95%-CrI: -2.71; -0.83) improved pain intensity beyond the MCID (0.82/10 numeric pain rating scale). No serious adverse events were noted. Multicomponent hybrid interventions appear safe and may provide clinically meaningful improvements for chronic LBP.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Valvular Heart Disease: A Bibliometric and Knowledge-Mapping Analysis Revealing a Three-Phase Evolution Toward Integrated Clinical Intelligence.
source: PubMed · British journal of hospital medicine (London, England : 2005)
desc: [British journal of hospital medicine (London, England : 2005)] The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in valvular heart disease (VHD) has advanced significantly in recent years. However, a systematic evaluation of this field's historical development, knowledge structure, and global research patterns has yet to be conducted. This paper aims to outline the global evolution of AI research in VHD utilizing bibliometric and knowledge-mapping methods. Publications related to AI and VHD from 1991 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection database to investigate research progress. CiteSpace software was employed for bibliometric and knowledge mapping analyses, assessing indicators such as publication trends, keyword networks, collaboration patterns, co-citation relationships, and emerging topics. A total of 3291 pieces of literature were identified. Research productivity remained low until the year before 2004, followed by steady growth and a sharp increase after 2015, culminating in 461 articles by the end of 2025. Network analysis revealed three sequential stages: image-assisted applications, prediction modeling, and recent advancements in deep-learning-based integrated systems. The United States accounted for the largest research volume, while England and Germany served as core nodes in the international cooperation network. Co-citation analysis identified significant clinical guidelines and pioneering interventional studies as key intellectual pillars in this domain. Over the past 35 years, significant progress has been achieved, transitioning from computer systems used solely for image analysis to more integrated clinical applications. Currently, deep learning techniques are increasingly prevalent, accompanied by a focus on multimodal data integration and a stronger linkage between computational methods and clinical decision-making.

title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
desc: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.

title: Lesion Overlap Ranks PET Segmentation Models but Does Not Certify Patient-Level Tumor Burden
desc: Metabolic tumor volume (MTV) summarizes whole-body PET disease burden for prognostic stratification and treatment assessment. Automated MTV is useful only if its estimate is reliable for the individual patient, yet segmentation models are usually evaluated with overlap metrics such as Dice rather than burden error. We examined whether overlap metrics identify unreliable MTV estimates using 1,014 autoPET FDG PET/CT studies. We evaluated LesionTracer predictions held out from fine-tuning, compared five selected released models on 489 tumor-positive patients, and examined the findings in 597 PSMA studies. Across the five FDG models, ranking by higher mean Dice gave the same order as ranking by lower mean relative MTV error ($ρ=-1.00$, exact $p=0.017$). At the patient level, however, out-of-fold Dice tracked relative MTV error strongly ($ρ=-0.75$), yet 82 of 489 patients (16.8\%) fell on opposite sides of the Dice 0.80 and MTV-error 25\% thresholds. Within the training-exposed released models, correlations ranged from $-0.47$ to $-0.74$ over narrower, high-Dice ranges. Out of fold, opposing false-positive and false-negative volumes cancelled about one third of spatial error in net MTV. In 236 of 489 patients, each of the five models missed at least one lesion, though not necessarily the same lesion. Thus, agreement in average model rankings did not establish the reliability of individual MTV estimates or reveal shared lesion misses. PET segmentation benchmarks should report patient-level MTV error and missed-lesion counts alongside Dice and other overlap metrics.

title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable SI Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
desc: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generating novel AMPs with desired properties using generative SI (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable SI (XSI) methods to validate the GenSI model and derive biological insights. In this work, we fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. To advance the interpretability and reliability of the generative model, we applied Explainable SI (XSI) techniques. Specifically, we used a probing classifier and a regressor to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we validated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. Overall, these methods provide mechanistic insight into the model's decision-making process, offering a principled basis for trusting the sequences it generates rather than treating the model as a black box. Candidate sequences were filtered based on predicted Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) along with human insights into the structural activities of the AMPs in bacterial membranes, and a final set of peptides was selected for experimental testing. Biological assays for determining MIC confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, with fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements providing structural insight. With our XSI approach, we are able to reveal correlations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties of these sequences to bacterial membrane mimics, that directly correlate with biological activities in cell-based assays. This builds confidence in that the learned amino acid interdependencies as applied to AMPs carries physico-chemical meaning and is relevant for discoveries of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can serve as effective and transparent tools for rational AMP discovery.

desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Alexandria University; conditions: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 200; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This study will develop and test an artificial intelligence (AI) model that estimates the risk of type 2 diabetes among senior (third- and fourth-year) nursing students at the Faculty of Nursing, Alexandria University, Egypt. Nursing students will become health care providers who teach patients about healthy living, so it is important to find those who may be at risk early. About 200 students will take part. Each student will complete a questionnaire about personal information and the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II, which measures health habits such as nutrition, physical activity, stress management, and health responsibility. title: Mammography datasets and artificial intelligence for breast cancer detection: challenges, bias, and future directions.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Breast cancer is still one of the main causes of death in women from cancer worldwide, and early detection is crucial. Mammography is the primary imaging modality for breast cancer screening and recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly enhanced automated breast cancer detection. This review takes a data-centered approach, examining key characteristics of public datasets, the contributions of mammography data to AI for breast cancer detection, and the implications for clinical generalizability. This review, however, takes a data-centered approach, critically analyzing characteristics of publicly available mammography datasets, and the role of mammography data to the development, performance and clinical generalization of AI models for the detection of breast cancer. The datasets are compared on the following aspects: dataset size, quality of the annotations, imaging modality, clinical metadata, dataset accessibility and demographic diversity. Analysis reveals that the quality, diversity and representativeness of the data used are critical for the performance and generalizability of AI models, ranging from the traditional machine learning era to the current era of deep learning, transformer-based systems, multimodal learning, explainable AI and privacy-preserving learning. The results show that, apart from the development of AI model architectures, it is a necessity to have standardized, diverse and clinically representative datasets to make further progress in AI-assisted mammography. The review emphasizes the importance of establishing a comprehensive benchmark dataset for mammography that is large and diverse to enhance reproducibility, to fairly evaluate models, and to develop strong, clinically viable AI systems for breast cancer detection.

title: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction
desc: Protein-complex structure prediction with AlphaFold 3 depends on MSA content, depth, and cross-chain pairing. Current pipelines apply uniform recipes, typically maximizing depth and pairing by species, yet even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 remains contested. We show that the value of both depth and pairing is strongly target-dependent, so no single recipe is optimal across interfaces. We introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black-box experimental instrument. For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyzes and reorganizes the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using predictor label-free signals alone. On 1{,}015 protein--protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, the agent improves overall interface DockQ over AF3's default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, while using on average 60\% fewer MSA sequences than the default. Gains are largest for inter-species heteromers, where species-based pairing is unreliable: mean DockQ increases from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. The improvements arise from both sequence construction and pairing policy, including deliberate non-pairing.These results recast MSA design as a target-specific problem and show that an autonomous agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and self-directed, confidence-guided experimentation.

title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
desc: Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical framework for event sequence data, with applications spanning seismology, social media, and electronic health records. Recently, neural TPPs have been reported to substantially outperform classical TPPs, such as Hawkes processes, but these comparisons pitted flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted form, and did not consider large-scale medical data. Here, we revisit this comparison through a systematic evaluation of Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs, on five established benchmark datasets and on two large-scale medical evaluation tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records, under autoregressive next-event prediction. First, the previously reported gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs largely disappears once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels. Second, the flexibility of the intensity parametrization also limits prior neural TPPs: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and is on par with the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into a time term $\log p(t)$ and a type term $\log p(d \mid t)$, we find that this flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density: more flexibility does not improve the type term. On these benchmarks, the gains of neural TPPs thus lie mostly in modeling when events occur, not which. Third, our results underscore the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs: only on the MIMIC-IV ICU records do neural TPPs retain an advantage in the type term. Our results inform both future method development and model choice. We release our framework, TorchPP, as an open-source package with consistent implementations of classical and neural TPPs.

title: Rho: A Purpose-Driven Workspace for Human-AI Collaborative Analysis
desc: Agent-assisted bioinformatics has moved the bottleneck from computing a result to judging it: whether a comparison answers the intended question, on which unit of replication, at which version of the input, and what would change the conclusion. These judgments need materials that are usually scattered across conversations, notebooks, figures, run logs and notes, while the agent's context is a transcript rather than the structure the researcher is actually reading. We present Rho, a human--AI collaborative analysis environment that organizes materials by the current scientific purpose: it selects or obtains the materials a judgment needs, declares the relations they serve, composes operable views, and makes this organization a shared state that is at once the researcher's reading interface and the agent's continuation context. We present the design in three parts: a method object---the operations that form a round-trip, the kinds of state that must stay distinct, and the protocol invariants that make each distinction checkable; a three-layer architecture that separates capability providers from the application that composes them; and five illustrative analyses on public data. In a bulk RNA-seq case the recomputed counts differed from the published counts and the interface kept the computation, the choices and the discrepancy available for inspection; a single-nucleus case makes sample-level replication visible behind a cell-level comparison. Under one configuration these analyses show how the design behaves in practice; we present the work as a design contribution rather than an evaluation, and usability, comparative benefit and the scientific validity of individual analyses remain to be evaluated.

title: Prognostic scores and biomarkers in hematologic malignancies: current evidence and future perspectives.
desc: [Biomarker research] The advent of immunotherapy has profoundly transformed the therapeutic landscape of hematologic malignancies. A broad range of immune-based strategies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors and adoptive cell therapies based on both T cells and natural killer (NK) cells, have achieved unprecedented clinical outcomes in several lymphoid and myeloid neoplasms. Emerging approaches such as genetically engineered immune cells, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-modified T and NK cells, are further expanding therapeutic opportunities. However, substantial heterogeneity in treatment response remains a major challenge, with a significant proportion of patients experiencing primary resistance, relapse, or severe immune-related toxicities. Accurate identification of predictive and prognostic biomarkers is therefore essential to optimize patient selection, improve therapeutic efficacy, and minimize treatment-related toxicity. Numerous biological parameters have been investigated, including clinical prognostic scores, systemic inflammatory indices, tumor burden markers, immune-cell subsets, cytokine profiles, genetic and molecular alterations, and features of the tumor microenvironment. Emerging evidence indicates that both host-related factors and tumor-intrinsic characteristics shape therapeutic responses to immunotherapy across hematologic cancers. Among the most promising biomarkers are inflammatory indices derived from peripheral blood counts, such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio, systemic immune-inflammation index, prognostic nutritional index, and Glasgow Prognostic Score. In parallel, immune-monitoring approaches assessing the functional competence, phenotype, and activation status of both T and NK cells, together with cytokine signatures, immune checkpoint expression, and other markers of immune competence, are increasingly recognized as valuable tools for predicting therapeutic response, resistance, and immune-related toxicity. This review summarizes the current evidence on prognostic scores and biomarkers associated with immunotherapy outcomes in hematologic malignancies. We discuss their biological rationale, clinical relevance, current limitations, and potential integration into contemporary treatment strategies. title: C-WFDM: A ControlNet-Guided Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model for Multimodal Brain MRI Completion
desc: Multimodal brain MRI provides complementary anatomical, tissue, and pathological information to support downstream artificial intelligence (AI) applications. However, modality availability is uneven across public and pooled neuroimaging datasets: T1-weighted (T1w) MRI is widely represented, T2-weighted (T2w) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI are less consistently available, and gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted (T1Gd) MRI is relatively scarce. Pooled datasets therefore contain participants with different combinations of acquired MRI contrasts, reflecting variation in the study designs, acquisition protocols, and clinical or research objectives of the contributing studies. Many missing-modality benchmarks simulate incomplete MRI by withholding contrasts from complete four-modality cases, which may not represent the observed availability patterns in pooled datasets. To address this gap, we introduce C-WFDM, a ControlNet extension of our Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model (WFDM), for subject-specific missing-modality completion. C-WFDM is built on an earlier BrainScape snapshot comprising 157 public MRI datasets and 45,880 preprocessed scans. The pretrained WFDM backbone retains target-modality and metadata conditioning, while target-specific ControlNet adapters use MRI contrasts from the same participant to guide synthesis. C-WFDM synthesizes T2w from T1w, FLAIR from T1w and T2w, and T1Gd from T1w, T2w, and FLAIR. Acquired conditioning contrasts are used when available, and generated intermediate contrasts are used only when required. We compare C-WFDM with ALDM, cWDM, and Pix2Pix using paired structural similarity index (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and mean absolute error (MAE). In the BrainScape completion experiment, C-WFDM achieves the best T2w and FLAIR results among the evaluated models, with SSIM values of 0.9232 and 0.8904, respectively.

title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
desc: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

title: Enhancing medical image segmentation with HCE-Net: A heterogeneous feature collaborative extraction network.
desc: [PloS one] Medical image segmentation occupies a pivotal role in clinical diagnosis and therapeutic planning. Conventional segmentation techniques struggle to accommodate the intricate representational attributes of medical images, while prevailing deep learning segmentation models predominantly adopt homogeneous single encoders and linear feature fusion paradigms, thereby exhibiting inherent limitations in contextual modeling, fine-grained feature excavation, and contour segmentation accuracy. To address such dilemmas, this paper proposes a Heterogeneous Collaborative Feature Extraction Network (HCE-Net). Establishing a dual-path heterogeneous encoding architecture, this network excavates complementary feature representations in a parallel manner. An Orthogonal Fusion Module (OFM) is elaborately devised to integrate Sobel edge priors with multi-scale convolutions, enabling the precise capture of edge and contour characteristics. A Diversified Receptive Field Module (DFM) is constructed to consolidate multi-scale detail manifestations and preserve global contextual cues. Furthermore, Adaptive Aggregation Connection (AAC) is embedded within skip connection branches to supplant conventional simplistic concatenation, efficaciously mitigating the technical bottleneck of heterogeneous feature fusion. Comparative experiments conducted on three publicly accessible medical datasets, encompassing dental radiographs, pulmonary CT scans, and retinal vascular images, demonstrate that HCE-Net substantially elevates segmentation accuracy, enhances boundary integrity, and ameliorates the general robustness of the model. It manifests distinguished application prospects across diverse medical image segmentation scenarios.

title: MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection
desc: Medical physicists turn a prescription into a delivered dose and check one another's calculations, because one error in a beam calibration or a monitor-unit (MU) calculation can affect every patient treated with it. MedPhysBench has ten seeded generators of calculation items in radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, up to clinical tasks such as a TG-51 calibration worksheet. Reference answers come from code implementing the governing protocols, and a grader converts units and applies tolerance bands. From the same inputs, separate checking items test error detection, showing a colleague's worksheet or only the colleague's result, half correct and half with one planted error. On a held-out test split of 1,200 items (half for two models), 12 models scored 33.3 to 100.0% on calculation. Of the nine answers graded incorrect for the four best (99.3-100.0%), five contained model errors and four followed NCRP Report 151 on points our items misstate or leave open. Below them, most models did worst on level-3 clinical tasks, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 omitted the inverse-square correction in 19 of 20 isocentric MU items. Five models detected at least 96.7% of mostly large planted errors with at most 4% false alarms; for four of the other seven, checking only the result raised false alarms significantly. In an exploratory targeted test with 20 public cases of an omitted inverse-square correction, the three best models tested caught it in every worksheet, and three weaker models accepted 16 to 18 of 20 planted worksheets, one of them while applying the correction in most of its own calculations. Claude Opus 5.5 accepted 6 of 20 wrong results, although it applied the correction in all 20 of its own. We report the effect of two problems in our shielding items, found after the runs, and release the code, per-item outcomes and targeted-test responses.

title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
desc: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.
