No harmful effects were reported.

title: A Large Language Model-Based System for Depression Symptom Identification: Iterative Qualitative Co-Design Studies.
desc: [JMIR formative research] AI technologies have considerable potential to support mental health practitioners in identifying depression symptoms. However, existing tools are often developed with limited practitioner involvement and evaluated primarily on technical performance, leaving questions of clinical relevance, ethical design, and practitioner trust insufficiently addressed. This study aimed to examine how iterative co-design with mental health practitioners can inform the development of an AI-based model for identifying depression symptoms, focusing on how practitioner input shaped its clinical relevance and ethical foundations across 2 design cycles. We conducted a 2-stage qualitative co-design study. In stage 1, we developed DepressionSymp 1.0, a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 model trained on the CounselChat dataset, identifying 5 symptom categories based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC-22) psycholinguistic framework, reviewed and discussed by 6 mental health practitioners during online co-design workshops. In stage 2, this feedback informed DepressionSymp 2.0, expanded to 10 symptom categories and reviewed by 8 further practitioners in a second round of workshops. Practitioners valued the structured symptom outputs for reducing cognitive workload and supporting intervention planning. In stage 1, indirect indicators such as social withdrawal, financial difficulties, and major life changes were often classified as lifestyle factors rather than symptoms; this informed the expansion to 10 categories in stage 2, described as clearer and more useful for preassessment. Risk categorization was identified as the most ethically sensitive aspect across both stages, alongside broader concerns including the lack of nonverbal information in text-based assessments, cultural and linguistic differences in symptom expression, and the potential for automation bias without sufficient human oversight. Iterative co-design with mental health practitioners is valuable for developing AI-based tools that are clinically relevant and ethically grounded, demonstrating how qualitative practitioner feedback can inform iterative model refinement and ethical design. Findings inform design implications around large language model (LLM) features, practitioner-in-the-loop oversight, and ethical considerations covering clinical standards, informed consent, and data governance. Future work should prioritize larger

title: Personas Are Not People: Identity as State, Not Attribute
desc: Synthetic populations, large sets of simulated people, are increasingly used in place of real people to pretest surveys, simulate users and communities, and evaluate AI systems. Each simulated person is defined by a persona, a written profile of fixed traits, demographics, and attitudes that a language model is instructed to act out. Every such system assumes that a person's identity is a stable attribute that behaves the same way in every situation the simulation presents. We show that this assumption is not a harmless simplification. Three decades of personality research find the opposite. How a given person behaves varies more across contexts than people vary from one another. Drawing on identity economics, which describes how different situations activate different identities and norms within the same person, we separate behavior into three parts, which are stable traits, the identity a context calls up, and the situation itself. We then prove, under two stated assumptions, that any simulation built on fixed personas, no matter how detailed the personas or how large the underlying model, cannot reproduce the part of a population's behavior that is specific to it and its circumstances. We propose a new evaluation criterion based on this result and a person-in-context design that can meet it in principle. We test one version on a naturalistic Reddit personality corpus and on a published clinical-trial recruitment survey of a community with documented distrust of medical institutions. The design does produce context-dependent behavior when tested directly, but in neither setting does it fully match the real population, and we show where it falls short. The consequence for practice is a risk that synthetic-population evaluations misrepresent the groups whose behavior is most shaped by context, a distortion that richer personas cannot correct.

title: CARTnet: Template-guided B-cell Epitope Prediction with Contact-aware Attention
desc: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.

title: Servier’s $1.6B muscular dystrophy bet on Edgewise delivers quick-fire pivotal failure
Use and Acceptability of an AI-Assisted Health Application for Individuals Living With a Chronic Condition
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Fondation Net-Care.ch; conditions: Hypertension, Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2, Obesity; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 1600; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The SOFIA study evaluates a web-based health application for people living with one or more chronic conditions. The study aims to find out whether the SOFIA application is useful, easy to use, and used over time by participants. The SOFIA application offers tools to support the day-to-day management of health: lifestyle challenges, health data entry and personal tracking (e.g., blood pressure, weight), medication tracking for people using pochettes-doses (pharmacy-prepared unit-dose packets), and an AI conversational assistant providing general health information. The application does not make diagnoses, give personalized medical advice, or recommend treatment. It complements usual medical care but does not replace it. The study first enrolls people with hypertension, then, subject to ethics committee approval, people with type 2 diabetes and obesity. Participation takes place entirely online, through the SOFIA application, accessible from a web browser (smartphone, tablet, or computer). There are no in-person visits. Participants use the application freely, at their own pace, until the end of the study. Short questionnaires (most take 1 to 3 minutes) are offered in the application during the study, and a final questionnaire (about 20 minutes) at the end.

title: Large language model developments.
desc: [Royal Society open science] Large language models (LLMs) are generative artificial intelligence (AI) models trained with vast amounts of data and context, and excel at processing, understanding and generating human language, using transformer models to learn statistical relationships between tokens. LLMs are a subset of transformer models, and hence are closely related but not interchangeable. Given the 'explosion' of LLM research, the challenge is tracking emerging developments and matching LLMs to applications. This paper reviews LLM developments with the aim of understanding the underlying models' computational strengths and weaknesses, building on previous work focusing on LLM optimization (Sharkey & Treleaven 2025 Optimising large language models: taxonomy and techniques. SSRN Scholarly Paper no. 5278456. Rochester, NY: SSRN). We find that despite their power, LLMs (transformers) face several key challenges. These include: (i) computational complexity and resource requirements-training and deploying large models is extremely costly and slow, and energy consumption is a concern; (ii) understanding long sequences and dependencies-even with enhancements, models can struggle with very long-range dependencies or context lengths beyond their window (e.g. maintaining coherence in a long document), which reflects the more fundamental absence of continual learning; (iii) interpretability and bias-it remains difficult to interpret why a model produces a given output, and models can inadvertently amplify biases present in training data; and (iv) optimization challenges, including fine-tuning for specific tasks without overfitting or losing generality and ensuring efficient inference (latency, the delay before a response is completed) for real-time applications. In summary, this review focuses on architectural, optimization and interpretability developments in LLMs. It does not aim to provide a systematic benchmark comparison, exhaustive implementation details or empirical performance evaluation, which are covered extensively elsewhere. The authors are committed to updating this review aligned to constant changes in the technology; please reach out with any additions.

title: Diagnosis by Composition: Detecting and Localizing Unseen Diseases by Composing Learned Radiological Findings
desc: Deep models for radiological diagnosis are typically trained to predict disease labels directly from images, which limits them to diseases seen during training and makes their decisions hard to interpret in radiologists' terms. Radiology, however, proceeds from visual findings to disease through published guidelines that make this decision rule explicit, interpretable, and reproducible. We introduce diagnosis by composition (DbC), a representation learning framework that encodes this findings-first logic. DbC learns a vocabulary of radiological findings by aligning image features with the text embeddings of the findings, each finding represented as a dense map over the scan. A disease is defined by a set of required findings derived from its guidelines, and its diagnosis map is a fixed, parameter-free composition of the corresponding finding maps. Because the finding-to-disease mapping is derived from guidelines rather than learned, DbC is interpretable and auditable by design, can extend to new diseases by specifying their findings without retraining, and can diagnose unseen diseases by composing their findings. On multi-phase liver CT, DbC detects and localizes unseen diseases, rare diseases from a different institution, and an external cohort significantly better than all comparators, including models that align images with disease names. DbC also improves detection and localization in the fully supervised setting and remains superior across training-set sizes. Although demonstrated on liver CT, DbC applies wherever radiological guidelines define diseases through findings.

title: All-Atom Structure Tokenizer: AtomLM-9b for Biomolecular Structure Prediction
desc: We develop an All-atom Structure Tokenizer that compresses biomolecular geometry into discrete structural tokens and achieves high-accuracy all-atom reconstruction. A hierarchical geometric encoder and finite scalar quantization map chemical units to a shared vocabulary of 8,192 tokens, while a joint coordinate de-tokenizer reconstructs backbone, side-chain, nucleic-acid, and ligand heavy atoms. The tokenizer achieves all-atom lDDT scores of 0.832 and 0.835 on CASP14 and CASP15, respectively. Building on this tokenizer, we train AtomLM-9b, an autoregressive language model based on Qwen3.5-9B that predicts structural tokens from molecular identities and connectivity and decodes them into complete atomic structures. We demonstrate, for the first time, protein structure prediction performance comparable to AlphaFold 3 with an all-atom-tokenizer-based structural language model: on the FoldBench protein-protein task, AtomLM-9b achieves a success rate of 75.01%, compared with the published AlphaFold 3 result of 72.93%. These results establish discrete all-atom tokenization as an effective interface between high-fidelity atomic reconstruction and language-model-based structure prediction.

title: Smith+Nephew held failed talks with J&J over potential orthopedics combination
Comparison of Two Patient Education Methods in Women With Chronic Low Back Pain: Online Pain Education vs. AI-Driven Patient Education on Pain Beliefs, Catastrophizing, and Self-Efficacy
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Amasya University; conditions: Chronic Low Back Pain (CLBP); type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 60; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The goal of this study is to learn if ChatGPT-generated answers can improve pain beliefs, catastrophizing, and self-efficacy in women with chronic low back pain compared to supervised pain education. The main questions it aims to answer are: Does ChatGPT improve pain beliefs, catastrophizing, and self-efficacy in women with chronic low back pain? Is ChatGPT as effective as supervised pain education? Participants will: complete baseline questionnaires online, attend a single 30-60 minute online session (randomly assigned to either a supervised pain education presentation or asking frequently questions about low back pain to ChatGPT)

title: Automation and artificial intelligence in the clinical microbiology laboratory.
source: PubMed · Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
desc: [Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology] Clinical microbiology laboratories face persistent pressure to shorten turnaround times, reduce manual workloads, and standardize diagnostic workflows. Total laboratory automation (TLA) and artificial intelligence (AI) are complementary responses to these demands. In this review, we examine how the evidence base for automation and AI in clinical microbiology is distributed along a maturity gradient and what this distribution implies for the next phase of implementation. Available evidence indicates that automated platforms shorten culture turnaround times and reduce manual workload in observational and multi-center studies, although the scale of benefit depends on specimen type and workflow configuration. Automated reading, identification, and susceptibility testing systems showed high concordance with manual standards for common specimen types, with error rates below commonly cited acceptability thresholds. Evidence for AI performance in plate reading and resistance prediction is abundant; however, most models remain in an assistive phase without prospective validation. Randomized trials of rapid testing and automation rarely demonstrate overall clinical superiority, and patient-oriented benefits remain limited and inconsistent. Guidelines provide directional support, whereas interoperability, quality control, and regulatory frameworks are still under development. The priority of the field is not additional single-center performance validation. The next phase requires multi-center prospective verification, interpretability, standardization, and comparative evidence with clinical outcomes as endpoints. AI-assisted evidence tools may accelerate evidence generation, although their utility remains preliminary.

title: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation
desc: Transfer learning from natural images is standard in supervised and increasingly adopted in self-supervised medical image analysis, but its role in generative modelling, and in particular diffusion denoisers, remains underexplored. Medical diffusion models typically train the denoiser from scratch, with no systematic evaluation of natural-image transfer. We analyse this across latent and pixel paradigms, model sizes (131M-952M) and two radiology datasets (RadImageNet, BraTS), and ask which aspects of transfer support generation. We find that: i) Natural-image initialisation consistently improves generation, by 21-34% relative gFID in pixel space against 14% in latent space, where the tokeniser supplies much of the prior. gFID gains mirror downstream pathology classification and radiomic-feature FD, both proxies for clinical fidelity. ii) Benefits reflect spatial structure, not semantics: semantic probing does not predict generation quality, whereas a spatial-structure metric adapted to internal denoiser representations tracks gFID at $|r|=0.85$, positioning spatial organisation as a channel through which pretraining manifests. iii) Mixed-domain denoiser training shows that natural and medical images share similar layer-wise representations up to the late blocks, and mixing natural images into medical training improves fidelity. iv) Transfer benefit is tied to natural image initialisation, outperforming in-domain medical pretraining and several reinitialisation schemes. Overall, natural image denoisers transfer positively to medical ones in our setup. Code is available at https://github.com/CAIROLab-Bern/rad-dit

title: Effect of a Web-based Application With Integrated AI Chat for Cardiovascular Risk Support
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Cairo University; conditions: AI Chatbot, Cardiovascular (CV) Risk; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 116; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] To determine the effect of a web-based application with an integrated AI chat module on 10-year cardiovascular risk score (intervention) versus usual clinic care (control) after 3 months from baseline score.

title: Head and neck pathology in India: Past, present, and future.
source: PubMed · The National medical journal of India
desc: [The National medical journal of India] We provide a snapshot of the development of the field of head and neck pathology in India. We take a look at the history from its origin in the early pre-Independence days and its journey through the growing years in the middle decades to its current stage. The landscape of head and neck pathology in India has been dominated by the pathology of oral squamous cancers, largely driven by tobacco-related carcinogens and influenced by habits, social, cultural, dietary and a multitude of epidemiological and genetic factors. Many head and neck pathologists, oral pathologists, surgeons, epidemiologists, molecular biologists-including Khanolkar, Sanghvi, Borges, and Daftary-have collaborated and shaped the narrative of head and neck pathology over many decades constantly driving the field forward. Over the years, the focus has widened from squamous cell cancers to expand to other subsites, including salivary gland, sinonasal pathology, recently described entities, molecular studies, and application of artificial intelligence for prediction and prognostication in head and neck pathology. Standing tall on the shoulders of the pioneers of pathology, the field of head and neck pathology in India has made long strides. While many challenges still remain, head and neck pathology in India is ready to leap into a brighter future.

title: Federated Transfer Learning for Medical Image Classification under Mixed Skew
desc: Deep learning in medical imaging is constrained by data scarcity and by privacy regulations that make centralizing patient data across institutions impractical. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these constraints by keeping data local, but its distributed nature exposes training to strong statistical heterogeneity. Multicentric medical data is particularly affected, exhibiting a mixed skew that combines feature, label, concept, and quantity shifts across centers. Personalized FL mitigates heterogeneity by tailoring a model to each client, yet most methods assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic given the high dimensionality of medical features relative to the limited data available. We propose the Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained (PAFP) framework, a personalized FL approach built on a pre-trained backbone. PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks to realign hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target. On the FedISIC benchmark, PAFP attains the highest unweighted balanced accuracy while reducing inter-client performance variance roughly six-fold relative to the strongest baseline, yielding accuracy and cross-client equity jointly. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Alexandre-Leclercq/PAFP.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Obstetricians, and Midwives in Non-Stress Test Interpretation
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Bilecik Seyh Edebali Universitesi; conditions: Non-Stress Test Interpretation, Fetal Well-Being Assessment; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 300; status: RECRUITING] This prospective observational study aims to evaluate and compare the interpretation of antenatal non-stress tests (NSTs) by three artificial intelligence models, three obstetricians, and three midwives. A total of 300 NST recordings obtained during routine antenatal care will be collected and prepared in PDF format. The recordings will be distributed to the evaluators, who will independently assess NST reactivity and recommend appropriate clinical management within two weeks. Two perinatologists will independently evaluate the NST recordings to establish the reference standard. In cases of disagreement, a third perinatologist will be consulted to determine the final reference assessment. The study will compare the diagnostic performance, agreement with the reference standard, and inter-rater agreement among artificial intelligence models, obstetricians, and midwives.

title: Artificial intelligence for the detection of large vessel occlusion stroke and workflow optimization: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
desc: [Journal of neurosurgical sciences] To evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) tools on workflow efficiency, treatment times, and clinical outcomes in patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke. We included observational studies that assessed the implementation of AI-based tools in the management of patients with suspected or confirmed LVO stroke. Eligible studies reported workflow, treatment, safety, or functional outcomes. Data were extracted on thrombolysis rates, CTA-to-arterial puncture time, door-to-puncture time, endovascular treatment (EVT) access, reperfusion success, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH), mortality, and functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days. Random-effects models were applied to calculate pooled mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Thirteen studies were included. AI implementation significantly reduced workflow delays: CTA-to-puncture time decreased by -40.20 minutes (95% CI -66.41 to -13.99; P<0.01) and door-to-puncture time by -23.17 minutes (95% CI -38.71 to -7.63; P<0.01). Thrombolysis administration showed no difference (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.57-1.09; P=0.15). Similarly, no significant effects were observed for EVT access (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.66-1.44; P=0.89), reperfusion success (RR 1.06; 95% CI 1.00-1.12; P=0.06), sICH (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.30-1.35; P=0.23), or mortality (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.38-1.37; P=0.32). However, AI-based workflows significantly improved functional independence at 90 days (RR 1.55; 95% CI 1.12-2.15; P=0.008). AI tools significantly improve treatment times and functional independence in acute LVO stroke without increasing adverse events.

title: A 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and segmentation
desc: Radiologists interpret computed tomography (CT) scans by jointly determining what a finding represents and where it lies in three-dimensional (3D) anatomy. However, CT models have treated CT interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, leaving textual findings spatially unverifiable and overlooking potential synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception. Here we present HoloCT, a generalist 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation by jointly modelling whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, providing 3D masks as evidence. We curated HoloDATA, comprising 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT-mask pairs. Across 346 tasks spanning segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation on 61 internal and 12 external datasets, HoloCT outperformed specialist and foundation models. In multicentre validation across 11,455 clinical CT scans from five hospitals, HoloCT outperformed competing models in lesion segmentation and report generation by 18.2 and 15.3 points. It also achieved 85.1% mean accuracy in screening thyroid tumours and colon lesions, exceeding all four participating radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Further analyses revealed bidirectional semantic-spatial synergy: language-guided segmentation delineated unseen anatomical structures and lesions as well as diffuse free-text findings, outperforming the leading approach by 22.1 points, whereas prompting the model to generate corresponding 3D masks alongside its textual outputs significantly improved interpretation performance. HoloCT shows that clinical understanding and spatial perception can be learned together within a single foundation model and offers a path towards more accurate and reliable CT analysis.

title: Evaluation of Large Language Models in Parasternal Block Ultrasound Interpretation
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Kanuni Sultan Suleyman Training and Research Hospital; conditions: Parasternal Block; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 32; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This prospective observational study aims to evaluate the accuracy of multimodal large language models (LLMs) in interpreting ultrasound recordings of superficial and deep parasternal intercostal plane blocks. Ultrasound recordings obtained during routine regional anesthesia procedures will be independently evaluated by LLMs using standardized prompts. Their ability to identify anatomical structures, assess local anesthetic spread, determine block success, and recognize potential procedural risks will be compared with expert anesthesiologist assessments. The study aims to investigate the potential role of LLMs in ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia assessment and clinical decision support.

title: Sycophancy and Extended Engagement with Publicly Accessible Generative AI: Aligning Deployment with Mental Health Needs.
desc: [Current psychiatry reports] Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a routine source of health information, emotional support, and companionship. As its use expands, the key public health question is not only whether these tools can support care, but whether their deployment is aligned with the mental health needs of the community. In this commentary, we argue that general-purpose AI systems pose distinct psychosocial risks, especially for young people and those experiencing loneliness or psychological distress. Emerging evidence suggests that sustained chatbot use may be associated with loneliness, reduced socialisation, emotional dependence, and problematic use, while sycophantic model behaviour may undermine users' capacity for self-correction and sustain a feedback loop of engagement. Current AI policy frameworks address governance and safety, but do not yet provide a coordinated response to these mental health risks. Realising the benefits of AI without preventable community-level harm will require independent longitudinal research, psychosocial safety benchmarking, transparent post-deployment monitoring, and safety by design principles.

title: CoRTeC: A Differentially Private Release for Synthetic Tabular Data, Decodable by Any Generator
desc: The records that could train the most useful models, such as a hospital's patient files, are often the ones an institution cannot share. We propose CoRTeC, a method that releases synthetic versions of such records under differential privacy. Differential privacy places a proven limit on what the synthetic data can reveal about any person, and in particular on membership inference. CoRTeC spends the privacy budget once, on a small file of noisy counts designed for training a classifier. For each group of records, the file gives the group's size, its balance of outcomes, a histogram of every column for each outcome and the outcome rate in each of several non-overlapping cells. A reviewer can check every number before the file leaves the institution. Anyone can then turn the counts into synthetic rows, as often as they like and at no further privacy cost. A maximum-entropy decoder can do this without any language model, and so can each of the five frozen language models we tested. None of them ever sees a real record. A selection step then matches the rows to the released counts. Decoded without a language model, the automatically configured release at $\varepsilon = 2$ trains classifiers to within 0.02 AUC of a real sample of the same size on the Adult dataset, across three data splits. On NHANES and bank marketing, without the selection step, it stays within 0.05 AUC. On Adult, with a fixed cohort rule, the release carries the outcome rates a deployment names more closely than a real sample does, at some cost in accuracy on pairs of columns. Four controls show that most of the utility comes from the release and the selection step, and that a language model adds what it knows from the column names. No private row ever reaches a model, and no row CoRTeC generates copies a real one. The strongest membership attack stays far below the bound the budget allows.

title: Artificial intelligence-empowered 4D bioprinting for craniomaxillofacial subunit reconstruction: a comprehensive review.
source: PubMed · Frontiers in bioengineering and biotechnology
desc: [Frontiers in bioengineering and biotechnology] Craniomaxillofacial subunit transplantation represents one of the most technically demanding reconstructive strategies for repairing anatomical subunit defects involving the cranium, mandible, maxilla, orbital cavity and nose. Conventional reconstructive approaches are hindered by inherent limitations in personalized anatomical matching, dynamic tissue adaptability, and long-term therapeutic efficacy. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and four-dimensional (4D) bioprinting has revolutionized craniomaxillofacial reconstructive surgery. This review summarizes state-of-the-art advances in AI-enabled 4D bioprinting for craniomaxillofacial subunit repair, covering core application scenarios including bone defect regeneration, facial soft tissue and cutaneous organ reconstruction, peripheral neural regeneration, and vascularized composite tissue fabrication. We elaborate the synergistic potential of AI and 4D bioprinting in craniomaxillofacial subunit reconstruction, and dissect critical bottlenecks including inadequate material performance, low precision of shape deformation programming, and limited clinical translatability of existing AI models. This work provides valuable insights for further translational research of AI-integrated 4D bioprinting in craniomaxillofacial subunit reconstruction.

title: PathoS2VD: From 2D Histopathology to Pseudo Z-Stack Representations
desc: For decades, diagnostic pathology has relied on thin two-dimensional (2D) tissue sections, despite biological tissues exhibiting inherently three-dimensional (3D) morphological organization. Because a single section captures only one focal plane, important morphological cues along the z-axis are inevitably discarded, limiting tissue representation for both human interpretation and computational analysis. In this work, we propose a generative framework that learns z-axis morphological priors from pathology z-stack data, offering a cost-effective alternative to dedicated volumetric imaging, and transfers this knowledge to conventional single-plane histopathology. Specifically, an image-to-video (I2V) latent diffusion model (LDM) is trained to synthesize a pseudo z-stack from a single 2D image, capturing plausible morphological variations across adjacent focal planes rather than reconstructing physical tissue volumes. To enable deployment on large-scale clinical datasets without native z-stack acquisition, we further introduce a prior-preserving mixture fine-tuning strategy that adapts the model to new domains while retaining the learned z-axis morphological prior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the synthesized pseudo z-stacks exhibit realistic cross-plane morphological continuity and consistently improve downstream prostate cancer classification compared with conventional 2D representations. Our results suggest that learning transferable z-axis priors from limited z-stack data provides a practical way to enrich routine pathology images with complementary morphological information. Code: https://github.com/QuIIL/PathoS2VD.

title: Adversarial robustness of deep learning-based thyroid nodule segmentation in ultrasound.
desc: [PLOS digital health] Deep learning-based segmentation models are increasingly integrated into clinical imaging workflows, yet their robustness to adversarial perturbations remains incompletely characterized, particularly for ultrasound images. We evaluated adversarial attacks and inference-time defenses for thyroid nodule segmentation in B-mode ultrasound. Two black-box adversarial attacks were developed: (1) Structured Speckle Amplification Attack (SSAA), which injects boundary-targeted noise, and (2) Frequency-Domain Ultrasound Attack (FDUA), which applies bandpass-filtered phase perturbations in the Fourier domain. Three inference-time mitigations were evaluated on adversarial images: randomized preprocessing with test-time augmentation, deterministic input denoising, and stochastic ensemble inference with consistency-aware aggregation. Experiments were conducted on a U-Net segmentation model trained on cine-clips from a database of 192 thyroid nodules. The baseline model achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.76 (SD 0.20) on unperturbed images. SSAA reduced DSC by 0.29 (SD 0.20), from 0.76 to 0.47, while maintaining high visual similarity (SSIM = 0.94). FDUA resulted in a smaller DSC reduction of 0.11 (SD 0.09), from 0.76 to 0.65, with lower visual fidelity (SSIM = 0.82). Against SSAA, all three defenses significantly improved DSC after correction, with deterministic denoising showing the largest recovery (+0.10, p < 0.001), followed by randomized preprocessing (+0.09, p < 0.001), and stochastic ensemble inference (+0.08, p = 0.002). No defense achieved statistically significant improvement against FDUA, although recall consistently improved at the cost of reduced precision. The tested inference-time defenses therefore partially mitigated spatial-domain perturbations, whereas statistically significant DSC recovery was not demonstrated against frequency-domain perturbations, highlighting attack-specific challenges in adversarial robustness evaluation.

title: 3D Banff Glomerulitis Scoring for Kidney Transplant Pathology: Feasibility Study for Volumetric Quantification
desc: Quantifying glomerular inflammation in kidney-transplant biopsies is traditionally performed on single whole-slide sections using the Banff "most-severe section" rule, despite the inherently three-dimensional nature of lesion distribution. This 2D based assessment might lead to instability when inflammation varies across slices. This paper reports a feasibility study examining the technical feasibility and clinical relevance of extending Banff scoring into three dimensions. To this end, we propose a 3D Banff lesion-scoring framework that aligns serial sections, reconstructs glomerular identities across depth, and integrates inflammatory-cell counts in 3D under three scoring strategies: Compatible, Volumetric, and Deduplicated Volumetric. In the experiments, glomerulitis (g-scores) was used as an example Banff metric and applied to multi-section renal allograft biopsies. Our findings indicate that 3D Banff g-scores are more consistent across sections and, under the semi-automatic setting, the Volumetric strategy correlates more strongly with clinical biomarkers than traditional 2D scores. These results show that 3D volumetric quantification offers promising added value, underscoring the potential benefit of 3D-aware Banff scoring for kidney transplant pathology.

title: An Application of the Self-Determination Theory Model for AI-Enhanced, Digital Psychosocial Interventions for Pediatric Disabilities.
source: PubMed · Western journal of nursing research
desc: [Western journal of nursing research] Youth with developmental disabilities (DDs) experience elevated psychosocial challenges, including difficulties with emotion regulation, self-concept, and access to timely mental health support. Pediatric nurses are well-positioned to address these needs; however, time constraints, limited training, and restricted access to specialty services often impede the provision of consistent psychosocial care. Digitally delivered psychosocial interventions enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI) offer new opportunities for individualized, accessible support, but these approaches frequently lack a clear theoretical foundation. This paper applied Self-Determination Theory (SDT), specifically Basic Psychological Needs Theory, to guide pediatric nurses' use of AI-enhanced, digital psychosocial interventions for DDs in practice. A theory-driven synthesis mapped SDT needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) to AI-enabled intervention features: conversational agents, neuro/adaptive feedback, and emotion-recognition tailoring. The framework specifies how these features can promote volitional engagement, optimal challenge with timely feedback, and supportive interactions for youth with DDs. It also notes evidence gaps (small, heterogeneous samples; limited comparisons and follow-up) and barriers involving payment/workload, equity and access, and data protection, transparency, and bias. SDT offers a coherent, testable foundation for designing, evaluating, and integrating AI-enhanced psychosocial supports for pediatric DDs. Nurses can screen for support, coach families, monitor risks, and advocate for ethical deployment and rigorous research.

title: VirtualTrialHarness: Coordinating Agentic Operationalization of Virtual Trial Protocols Across Complex Clinical Schemas
desc: Virtual trials use routinely collected clinical data to evaluate treatment strategies, but translating a study protocol into an executable analysis requires determining how clinical concepts and study requirements should be represented in the available data and applied consistently across the workflow. These decisions depend on local data representations and operational conventions and can involve source selection, patient and encounter identity, linkage, and temporal interpretation. Here we introduce VirtualTrialHarness (VTHarness), an agent framework that coordinates virtual-trial operationalization by selecting reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to maintain consistent study decisions across stages. We also introduce VTBenchmark for evaluating source selection and cohort construction. Across three complex synthetic environments, VTHarness successfully produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in 95.1% of workflows after requirement clarification, compared with 60.4% using retrieval from the same procedural corpus. Procedural skills improved source recovery across three language models and increased source overlap with analyst code in 13 Mayo Clinic cases. Site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks. Within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program, the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis. These findings support coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions to improve virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas.

title: Deep-Reorder: Refined Motion Correction for 3D Brain MRI via Iterative Data Regrouping.
desc: [Magnetic resonance in medicine] Accurate and temporally high-resolution estimation of subject motion is paramount for effective motion-correction in MRI. This work proposes a novel approach for estimating subject motion within a 3D MRI scan with high temporal resolution. Starting from an incoherent sampling scheme, images are reconstructed from temporally ordered k-space fractions via deep learning, enabling motion estimation via registration between each image. Assuming the bulk of the motion is removed using these initial estimates, the remaining misalignment between k-space fractions is expected to be minimally correlated in time. Based on this insight, an iterative strategy is proposed in which shots are arbitrarily regrouped into new k-space fractions, regardless of their original temporal ordering, for subsequent motion estimation and correction. This effectively increases the temporal resolution of the approach, enabling individual correction of all shots. When applied to 3D T1w TFE MRI of the brain, the proposed approach "Deep-Reorder" estimated a unique motion state for all shots, producing significantly better estimations of retrospective motion compared to estimation without iterative data regrouping. On prospectively motion-corrupted scans with intentional head movement by volunteers, the proposed approach consistently improved image quality, producing less noisy images with reduced motion artifacts. In conclusion, the proposed approach, which is free of external tracking devices or navigators, effectively estimated 3D motion and corrected motion artifacts with increased temporal resolution.

title: Weight-space programming for auditing clinical decision networks
desc: Machine learning models in radiotherapy are commissioned by testing them on cases with known answers, which may not reveal a shortcut that the test cases share with the training data. Frontier language models have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of small neural networks, an ability called weight-space programming. The purpose of this study was to determine whether such a model, given only a clinical protocol and a network's weights, can audit and repair the network. Networks with 433 to 4,801 parameters were trained to screen head-and-neck planning requests against four rules. Flaws were planted through the training data: confounds that hid each rule, a 3 Gy shift in the cord threshold, and a hidden trigger. Claude Opus 5.5 audited each network blind, without tools, data or code execution, and every claim and repair was tested on about 420,000 requests. The language model named the broken rule in 16 of 18 flawed networks (95% CI 67% to 97%), including all 15 with a confound or a threshold shift. It repaired each of the 16 by changing a median of 3 parameters. Fine-tuning on protocol-labeled requests also repaired every network, but changed nearly every parameter. Each confound and shift it found was visible in single units, and a simple statistic chosen for each flaw type found the same flaws. It cleared 2 of 5 healthy networks without being forced and found 1 of 3 triggers. Testing against the protocol detected every flaw, and black-box testing found the confounds and the shift faster. The results indicate that, in small networks, weight-space programming can locate and repair flaws that silence an input or shift a threshold, but cannot yet certify that a network is correct.

title: Food-Derived Anti-inflammatory Peptides: Mechanistic Evidence, AI-Assisted Discovery, and Process-Aware Preparation.
source: PubMed · Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
desc: [Journal of agricultural and food chemistry] Food-derived anti-inflammatory peptides (AIPs) are increasingly recognized as promising functional food ingredients, yet their reported bioactivities are often insufficiently linked to phenotypic outcomes, molecular mechanisms, and food-processing conditions. This review summarizes major inflammatory pathways relevant to orally delivered AIPs, including pattern recognition receptors, NF-κB/MAPK signaling, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, Keap1/Nrf2-mediated redox regulation, epithelial barrier integrity, macrophage remodeling, and inflammation resolution. Representative peptides are discussed in relation to sequence motifs, target-associated assays, enzymatic release, enrichment strategies, and marker-peptide verification. Reliable mechanistic assignment requires convergent evidence from pathway-specific readouts, cytotoxicity and endotoxin controls, gastrointestinal stability, and synthetic peptide validation. We further highlight AI-driven discovery using mechanism-annotated, release-aware data sets and propose a process-aware framework integrating motif-guided enzymatic hydrolysis, physicochemical fractionation, marker-peptide quantification, and process fingerprinting. Future advances depend on standardized validation, protein source traceability, safety and sensory profiling, and compatibility with food matrices.

title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
desc: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Generative Science of Food Formulation.
source: PubMed · Annual review of food science and technology
desc: [Annual review of food science and technology] Food formulation requires balancing taste, nutrition, sustainability, and cost. Traditionally, new foods have emerged through empirical experimentation, expert intuition, and iterative refinement. Now, artificial intelligence (AI) offers the opportunity to accelerate this process. Yet despite rapid advances across food science, most AI applications remain isolated prediction and optimization tasks rather than parts of a broader scientific approach. Here we integrate these emerging technologies into a unified framework-the generative science of food formulation-in which digital food representations enable AI to predict, discover, generate, organize, simulate, and optimize. We illustrate this approach through sustainability and nutrition, where generative AI transforms environmental and nutritional metrics from post hoc evaluation criteria into explicit design objectives. Finally, we identify the data, models, benchmarks, and automation that will establish computational food design as a rigorous scientific discipline. Together, these advances have the potential to transform food formulation from an empirical discipline into a generative science.

title: Fairness Metrics based on the AUC in Clinical Predictive AI
desc: Fairness evaluation of clinical prediction models for binary outcomes often involves fairness metrics that compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, or c-statistic) across subgroups. However, the AUC has been shown to be a non-collapsible metric, meaning that its subgroup specific and overall values are not directly comparable as often implicitly assumed. This raises important questions about how existing AUC-based fairness metrics should be used and interpreted. We examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics proposed in the literature, including: within-group AUC parity; cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity; gap-to-overall AUC; equity-scaled AUC; minimum-based metrics; $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$; $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$; and $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ or $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ parity. We characterise their estimands, relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC (into within- and cross-group components), and critically appraise them. We then illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the EuroSCORE II, a clinical prediction model for in-hospital mortality. We recommend reporting an AUC matrix, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, alongside population characteristics. When fairness metrics are needed, we recommend reporting the within-group AUC parity, with cross-group AUC parity providing supplementary information but requiring caution due to its potential conflict with calibration. Metrics involving $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ and $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ have merit, summarising within- and cross-group AUCs into single values, but their interpretation is non-trivial, and they should be used with caution. Gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC, and minimum-based metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and it is unclear how to operationalise them, making them not fit for purpose and generally not recommended.

title: Chemistry-informed AI for food toxicant and adulterant detection: matrix-aware validation and auditable decision support.
desc: [Food chemistry] Food toxicants and adulterants pose interconnected safety, authenticity, and regulatory challenges across complex food matrices. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) converts spectra, images, chromatographic-mass-spectral fingerprints, biosensor outputs, and portable-device signals into screening decisions. Toxicant detection is treated primarily as a threshold-based task, whereas adulteration is addressed as an authenticity or anomaly-detection problem. Evidence is evaluated using AI performance and classical analytical criteria, including selectivity, recovery, precision, robustness, limits of detection and quantification, measurement uncertainty, matrix effects, independent validation, and agreement with reference methods. The review distinguishes direct analyte evidence from correlated proxy signals and separates experimentally demonstrated methods from author-proposed chemistry-informed concepts. A matrix-aware framework links field screening with confirmatory laboratory analysis through calibration transfer, drift monitoring, uncertainty-based decisions, and traceable model records. Emerging tools, including conformal prediction, generative augmentation, digital twins, and secure ledgers, remain promising but are not yet fully validated for regulatory use in foods.

title: Matched but Not Better: An Equivalence-Tested Benchmark of Quantum Machine Learning on Six Clinical Datasets and the QML-Health-READY Reporting Framework
desc: Background: Quantum machine learning (QML) is promoted for clinical prediction, but comparisons with classical models are rarely paired or tested for equivalence. Methods: We compared a quantum-kernel support vector machine (QSVM; 4 qubits, tuned bandwidth) and a variational quantum classifier (VQC) with five tuned classical models across six public clinical datasets. All models used identical four-component inputs and 25 cross-validation splits. Paired AUROC differences were assessed using a corrected resampled t-test, Holm-adjusted equivalence tests (margins: +/-0.02 and +/-0.05), and random-effects pooling. Ablation, noise, finite-shot, and implementation-fault analyses were conducted. We propose QML-Health-READY, an eight-domain reporting framework. Results: Neither quantum model significantly outperformed any classical comparator. Pooled across datasets, QSVM differed from the kernel-matched radial basis function (RBF) SVM by -0.006 AUROC (95% CI: -0.017 to +0.004), equivalent to +/-0.02. VQC differed from the best classical model by -0.007 (95% CI: -0.019 to +0.004). QSVM was equivalent to RBF SVM within +/-0.05 in four of six datasets but was significantly worse than the best classical model on NHANES 2017-18 (-0.076). A classically trivial product-state kernel performed as well as the entangling kernel. With depolarizing noise (p = 0.01) and 1,024 shots per kernel entry, QSVM AUROC decreased by 0.054 (95% CI: 0.036 to 0.071). Untuned bandwidth produced near-chance AUROC (0.48-0.59). Conclusions: Correctly configured quantum classifiers approached but did not exceed tuned classical models. Finite-shot estimation, rather than gate noise, was their main practical cost, while configuration errors could reverse conclusions. QML-Health-READY defines reporting requirements for credible claims.

title: From Nano-Design to Field Deployment: An AI-Enabled Framework for Precision Agriculture.
source: PubMed · Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
desc: [Journal of agricultural and food chemistry] Functional nanotechnologies can improve agrochemical delivery, nutrient-use efficiency, and plant stress monitoring, yet their performance often varies under heterogeneous field conditions. This perspective proposes a three-stage, AI-enabled framework integrating predictive nanoformulation design, adaptive field deployment, and feedback-driven optimization. AI integrates material properties with soil, plant, climatic, and field-performance data while supporting ecological risk assessment and compatibility with precision application systems. Key challenges include limited field-scale data sets, model transferability, sensing reliability, standardization, regulatory uncertainty, and economic feasibility. Integrating material engineering with data-driven decision-making may enable more precise, adaptive, and environmentally responsible deployment of agricultural nanotechnologies.

title: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification
desc: Background/Objectives: CNNs perform well in retinal disease classification from spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), but whether EfficientNet's natural-image scaling hierarchy transfers to medical-image transfer learning at fixed resolution remains unclear. This study evaluates EfficientNet-B0-B7 for four-class SD-OCT classification and accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Methods: Eight ImageNet-pretrained variants (4.05-64.10M instantiated backbone parameters) were evaluated at 224x224 on the Kermany dataset. Grayscale images were replicated to RGB and processed using model-embedded preprocessing and augmentation. Training comprised frozen-backbone head training followed by partial fine-tuning. Metrics covered classification, discrimination, efficiency, and visual analyses. Results: Test accuracy varied non-monotonically from 95.93% (B0) to 96.95% (B1); B7 achieved 96.73%. B1 had the highest accuracy and Drusen F1 (0.8780), while B7 had Drusen F1 of 0.8720 and the highest Drusen recall (0.9177). Drusen had the lowest F1 across all variants and contributed 82.2% of the summed squared deviation in class-specific F1; class ranking remained Normal > CNV > DME > Drusen. The OCT accuracy ranking differed from the reported ImageNet hierarchy, where B7 ranked first. The accuracy-to-parameter ratio fell from 19.82 to 1.48 percentage points per million total parameters. The final train-test gap had a weak, non-significant association with test accuracy (r = 0.26, p = 0.53). Conclusions: Larger EfficientNet variants did not consistently improve SD-OCT classification. B1 achieved the highest accuracy and Drusen F1, whereas B7 showed a secondary accuracy recovery at greater model size and CPU latency, indicating task and protocol dependent scaling effects. As cross-partition duplicates have not been independently audited, results are conditional on the supplied split.

title: Deep-learning side-channel analysis of embedded ML-KEM: Single-trace message recovery, cross-device generalization, and frequency-band leakage characterization.
desc: [PloS one] Quantum computing undermines traditional public-key cryptosystems like RSA and ECC, prompting NIST to standardize Module Lattice Key Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) as a core Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) scheme in August 2024. Despite its theoretical security, ML-KEM's practical vulnerability in embedded systems remains underexplored. This study evaluates ML-KEM on an ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller under deep learning(DL)-based side-channel attacks (DL-SCA), revealing that a single power trace enables 32-byte message recovery with 99.98% accuracy, while cross-device testing across three chips achieves over 99% accuracy, highlighting critical DL-driven threats. To better understand the spectral characteristics exploited by deep-learning-based side-channel attacks, we conduct a controlled frequency-band sensitivity study using Butterworth and Chebyshev low-pass filters applied to recorded traces. Across different cutoff frequencies and filter orders, the validation accuracy decreases substantially under aggressive attenuation, indicating that a significant fraction of exploitable leakage resides in higher-frequency components. Rather than claiming that offline digital filtering constrains a realistic adversary, we interpret these results as evidence for where leakage-sensitive information is concentrated, thereby providing guidance for implementable countermeasures such as masking, shuffling, desynchronization, and acquisition-path power/EM conditioning in embedded PQC systems. This cost-efficient solution requires no algorithm/hardware modifications, emphasizing the urgency of implementation-level protections for secure PQC deployment in resource-constrained systems.

title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
desc: Foundation models for electroencephalography (EEG) are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours of recordings, and their accuracy grows with that amount. Such data is hard to assemble. The largest sources are clinical archives that cannot be redistributed, and the public sources are spread over several archives, file formats, and licences. We release eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets, as the gated Hugging Face dataset EEGDash/eegdash-corpus-v0 with the SHA-256 of every file. REVE, the largest published EEG foundation model, names 89 datasets as its pretraining corpus. Twelve cannot be redistributed: four clinical archives that hold 82% of its hours, and eight under no-derivatives licences. The corpus holds the 76 others that REVE's sampling rate allows and one more from REVE's release card: 77 datasets, 14,075 hours from 7,272 subjects, 5.0 million 10-second samples and 6.21 billion tokens per epoch. Every dataset is fetched through EEGDash, converted once with REVE's recipe, and stored in its own buckets of a chunked Zarr store with its licence recorded beside it, so a model can train on the whole store or on any subset of datasets. To test that the store pretrains a model, we retrain REVE-Base from scratch twice with the authors' code, changed only in how it reads data, and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. It reaches 0.331 under linear probing and 0.273 after fine-tuning, against 0.333 and 0.325 for the released model and 0.200 and 0.205 for an untrained encoder. The converter, the conversion reports, and the loader changes are released with the corpus.

title: Switchable hydrophilicity solvents and biosolvents for green microextraction in bioanalysis.
desc: [Bioanalysis] Sample preparation is critical in bioanalysis because of complex biological matrices and low analyte concentrations. Conventional liquid-liquid and solid-phase extraction are effective but often consume substantial organic solvents and resources. Green analytical chemistry has therefore promoted miniaturized microextraction approaches that reduce solvent use and waste while maintaining analytical performance. This review critically examines bioanalytical microextraction through two intersecting solvent-design perspectives: stimulus-responsive switchability and renewable/bio-derived solvent design, focusing on switchable-hydrophilicity solvents (SHSs) and bio-derived deep eutectic solvents (DESs)/natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs). SHSs enable reversible changes in hydrophilicity or ionic character to facilitate extraction and phase separation, whereas bio-derived DES/NADES systems provide tunable alternatives to conventional petroleum-based solvents. Their analytical performance, matrix-related challenges, reproducibility, and greenness are critically assessed. Future developments are expected to emphasize automated and miniaturized platforms, life-cycle assessment, and computationally assisted solvent design. Although molecular simulations are increasingly used to support solvent selection, predictive COSMO-RS and artificial-intelligence approaches remain emerging directions in bioanalysis.

title: Text-Only Domain Adaptation for Low-Resource Medical ASR: Shallow Fusion and Density Ratio Rescoring for Hausa
desc: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often struggle with specialised medical vocabulary, especially in low-resource languages where domain-specific speech data are scarce. We investigate text-only domain adaptation for Hausa medical ASR using the fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model and two decoding-time language-model fusion methods: Shallow Fusion (SF) and the Density Ratio Approach (DRA). A 4-gram KenLM trained on 19,421 Hausa health sentences serves as the medical target model, while a 75,372-sentence general-domain model provides the source prior for DRA. Evaluation uses 250 recordings of 25 physician-reviewed prompts from 10 speakers across six northern Nigerian states. Under prompt-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, SF and DRA reduce WER from 29.56% to 23.55% and 23.33%, respectively. Both significantly outperform greedy decoding (p < 0.001), while their difference is not significant (p = 0.423). However, general-LM-only SF achieves 23.96% WER, indicating that the medical LM's additional improvement over a general LM is modest. Medical Term Error Rate also improves under fusion, but does not establish a distinct medical-domain advantage. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, text-only language-model fusion can improve Hausa medical ASR without additional domain-specific speech collection.

title: Mitigating Spurious Invariance in Contrastive Learning: A Probabilistic Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Medical Image Analysis
desc: Owing to the prohibitive cost of manual annotation for enormous medical images, self-supervised learning (SSL) has gained substantial attention and shown promise in various medical imaging tasks. Among SSL approaches, contrastive learning has emerged as a prominent one, encouraging models to encode semantic information that remains invariant between different augmented views. However, this invariance can be spurious for medical images, as subtle but critical medical features can be suppressed during augmentations. In this paper, we mitigate this issue by encoding the learned feature embeddings as probability distributions rather than fixed vectors, thus capturing a richer and more nuanced spectrum of information. Furthermore, we propose a unified probabilistic framework that seamlessly integrates multiple SSL approaches. Our method achieves superior performance over the state-of-the-art SSL methods on various downstream tasks across multiple datasets, including medical image segmentation and classification. We further validate the method through additional analyses of robustness to stronger augmentations, label efficiency under limited fine-tuning labels, and computational trade-offs. The code is released at https://github.com/wwzjer/ProbSSL.

title: When can multi-fragment 2D/3D registration be trusted? Calibrated certification and uncertainty-driven view planning for pelvic fracture fluoroscopy
desc: Registering a segmented CT to fluoroscopy can locate every fracture fragment but can guide surgery only when trusted. After each shot, our closed loop registers all fragments, bounds their errors with a calibrated sandwich covariance, flags implausible or ambiguous ones, and stops or plans the next view. On simulated fluoroscopy of 60 held-out fracture CTs with realistic image uncertainty, 95% bounds covered 83% of unflagged fragments and 91% of those within 5mm, but from the second view on 14% failed by over 5mm, a third with bounds of at most 2mm. A fragment's shift when a view was added separated tightly bounded failures best (exploratory; AUC 0.94, bound 0.81). Requiring that the newest view moved no fragment beyond its bound, preferred post hoc, lowered false stops at 2mm from 23% to 6% overall, with 345 instead of 362 correct ones but more trajectories uncertified; delaying the stop did not, and other signals at equal acceptance left 10-15% false. With a segmentation error shared by all views (median Dice 0.89), 21% of this rule's stops were false against 10% without it (15 cases; exploratory). Minimax planning certified sooner than the clinical protocol without the check (4.20 versus 4.72 shots, Holm p <0.001), but no criterion reached the pre-specified endpoint, a true 2mm error, significantly sooner, even in the true basin. On real fluoroscopy of five intact pelves no 2mm certificate was false. Trust takes evidence across views, not only a calibrated local bound.

title: CAPTOR: text-encoder-free grounding by counting caption co-occurrence over the visual words of a frozen encoder
desc: Grounding a text query in an image needs a matrix scoring every term against every patch. Vision-language models compute it with an aligned text encoder, which many image encoders, such as histopathology-related models trained on slides alone, lack. The Caption-Anchored Patch-Term Occurrence Representation (CAPTOR) estimates the matrix without a text encoder. It clusters a frozen image encoder's patch tokens into visual words and describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word. A term signature is the standardized difference of those shares between images whose captions mention the term and the rest. The matrix factorizes into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor, so an image is encoded once and a new term adds one table row. Against every training-free baseline, CAPTOR leads on Common Objects in Context (COCO), Pascal Visual Object Classes (VOC) and Cityscapes. On COCO, scored on the cells one object owns, it reaches 0.565 mean intersection over union (mIoU) against 0.502. On all three, it is also level with a text alignment trained on the same backbone, which needs gradients, a text encoder and several times the captions. On held-out breast-cancer slides, it exceeds the strongest baseline scoring patches with a pathology text encoder by 0.160 mIoU. Read through CAPTOR, UNI, an encoder trained on slides alone, exceeds such baselines by 0.132 on a common grid. Counting can therefore give a text interface to any image encoder trained without language, wherever captioned images exist.

title: Recasting Visual Language Models as EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Neurodiagnostics
desc: Historically automated electroencephalography (EEG) systems was done using task-specific supervised models trained on purposely annotated data. A more recent modeling paradigm relies on creating a unified representation, or a 'foundation model', for multiple modality-specific tasks through large-scale domain-specific pretraining on the unannotated EEG signal. The quality of this unified representation directly depends on the availability of the modality-specific datasets. At the same time, generalist Vision Language Models (VLMs) exhibit broad few-shot learning capacities as well as good fine-tuning adaptability to different visual and language tasks. Can VLMs learn how to read and interpret EEG visually, emulating to a degree the way human clinicians inspect the EEG patterns? In this work we make a case that they can: we show that generalist VLMs without large-scale EEG pretraining perform competitively across a collection of clinical neuro-diagnostic tasks, can adapt to different tasks in a few-shot learning setting better than specialist foundation models, and exhibit better performance with model scaling when modality-specific models fail to exhibit.

title: OpenBrain: An Auditable Generated-Label Release for Whole-Brain MRI Parcellation
desc: Automatic tools can now generate whole-brain MRI parcellations at cohort scale, but generated-label releases often provide little evidence about which cases are reliable enough to reuse. We introduce OpenBrain, a confidence-aware release of 35,838 provenance-verified OpenNeuro T1w cases from 607 source datasets. OpenBrain is organized as an auditable case-record release rather than a directory of standalone segmentation files: each record links a primary parcellation, two committee parcellations, source/license provenance, raw QC-7 measurements, percentile risks, a combined risk score R, and a confidence tier. QC-7 is a reference-free reliability panel over label geometry, image-label consistency, and committee disagreement, so users can filter, weight, audit, or re-threshold generated labels without rerunning inference. We evaluate this released evidence under a frozen protocol. Across external cohorts, lower QC-7 risk corresponds to higher generated-label quality; in fixed-budget training, lower-risk selections improve paired macro Dice over random selection by +3.2 to +3.7 percentage points. OpenBrain also exposes raw axes, committee outputs, provenance, and datasheet documentation, so confidence claims remain inspectable after download. It does not turn generated labels into manual annotations or clinical-grade segmentations. Its contribution is a large open generated-parcellation substrate, a reusable case-level risk-evidence layer, and an external validation protocol for release-time QC. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/lanqz7766/OpenBrain. Code: https://github.com/lanqz7766/openbrain.

title: High-Resolution Quantitative MRI Using Contrast-Domain Multiscale Energy (MuSE) Regularization
desc: Quantitative MRI methods can offer tissue parameter maps (e.g. T1) that are comparable across scanners, sessions and subjects, together with multiple contrast-weighted images from a single scan. However, most data are acquired at 1 mm, which limits their use in neurodegenerative diseases that affect fine brain structures. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first diffusion-model-based reconstruction for quantitative MRI at 0.5 mm isotropic resolution from scans of less than 5 minutes, which has eightfold smaller voxel volume than clinical protocols. The key idea is to apply the prior to the synthesized contrast images rather than to the subspace coefficients. The prior is then independent of the temporal basis and the sequence, which improves generalization and allows a 2-D multiscale energy (MuSE) model trained on grayscale CelebA face images to be used without any MRI training data. The explicit energy makes reconstruction MAP estimation by a step-size-free majorize-minimize algorithm that regularizes a rotating subset of contrasts along different axes, which makes 3-D multi-contrast reconstruction tractable. For 3-D radial MPnRAGE at 7 T in 4.3 min, MuSE reduced the phantom NRMSE from 0.133 (CG-SENSE) and 0.091 (L1-wavelet) to 0.074 and the WM T1 interquartile range from 117 and 47 ms to 38 ms, and it was demonstrated in vivo at 7 T.

title: Dual-VaDE: Efficient and Robust Prototype Learning via Variational Dual-Domain Mixture Priors
desc: In this paper, we propose Dual-VaDE, an unsupervised generative framework for learning interpretable anatomical prototypes from unlabeled medical images. In contrast to previous variational methods that rely on a single spatial latent code, which often entangles global geometry with local textures and fails to capture their cross-domain dependencies, Dual-VaDE introduces a dual-domain Gaussian mixture prior that explicitly couples spatial anatomy with phase-preserving Fourier spectral representations. We derive an exact, closed-form variational lower bound that fuses this joint prior into the decoder and optimizes the entire network end-to-end via an alternating EM formulation, avoiding heuristic two-stage clustering while ensuring superior training stability and robustness. Evaluated on OASIS-3 brain MRI, Dual-VaDE delivers substantially sharper and more plausible prototypes, achieves superior cluster separation with improvements of up to 94% over spatial-only baselines, exhibits markedly reduced variance across random seeds, and incurs negligible inference overhead (0.28 ms per image).

title: Can saliency maps flag chest radiograph classifier errors at a new hospital? An external validation study
desc: Saliency maps are offered as a safeguard for medical image classifiers, but whether they reveal individual errors at a new hospital remains largely untested. We trained a convolutional network and a vision transformer on NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated 303,768 decisions per model at the training hospital and at two external sites, in the USA and Vietnam, with radiologist-consensus labels. We scored each explanation by its anatomical enrichment, the area-normalized concentration of attribution in a segmented thoracic region, and tested whether it detects errors beyond the model's confidence. Grad-CAM localized findings less often than radiologists (hit rate at most 0.575 versus 0.888). Adding enrichment to a confidence-based error detector calibrated at the training hospital never raised its area under the curve by more than 0.011, and for the convolutional network the relation between enrichment and correctness reversed between hospitals, degrading the transferred detector. Model confidence, not saliency, should anchor deployment monitoring.

title: Diffusion Plug-in Priors for Self-Supervised Ultrasound Video Restoration
desc: Ultrasound videos are limited by hardware-constrained spatial resolution and signal-dependent speckle, while paired low- and high-resolution acquisitions for supervised restoration are rarely available. We aim to jointly super-resolve and despeckle ultrasound videos without paired training data or network retraining. We propose UltraDiff, which uses a frozen pre-trained diffusion model (DM) as a plug-in prior and restores each frame by optimizing the latent seed of the DM sampler under a range-constrained maximum a posteriori formulation. We derive a speckle-aware data-fidelity term from a Rayleigh scale-family model and characterize its relative-residual and variance-adaptive weighting properties. We further introduce a stabilized fidelity that is bounded below and strictly convex in log intensity for positive observations in its unclamped form. A total-variation regularizer complements the DM prior, and a temporal seed update warm-starts each frame from the optimized seed of its predecessor. On EchoNet-LVH videos with simulated speckle and additive noise, UltraDiff with a natural-image prior improves PSNR by 1.24\,dB over the strongest baseline, and ultrasound-related priors improve it further. On real clinical echocardiography videos, UltraDiff reduces the mean absolute error of zero-shot ejection fraction (EF) prediction from 7.31 to 6.37 EF points relative to DUP, the strongest baseline. Combining a speckle-aware fidelity with frozen diffusion priors enables ground-truth-free ultrasound video restoration that benefits downstream measurement. UltraDiff needs neither paired data nor retraining and is not tied to a specific diffusion checkpoint. Code associated with this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: EP-LVMQA: Evidence-Preserving Coarse-to-Fine Localization for Low-Quality Long Video Moment Question Answering
desc: Long instructional videos are increasingly used in medical education, industrial training, and procedural knowledge transfer, yet their evidence is often incomplete or unreliable: subtitles may be missing, ASR noisy, OCR sparse, and decisive actions briefly shown without narration. Existing VideoQA systems typically return labels or free-form text, making answer support difficult to inspect. We study Long Video Moment Question Answering (LVMQA), where a system returns timestamped answer-supporting evidence. We propose EP-LVMQA, an evidence-preserving coarse-to-fine framework comprising an Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Evidence Timeline, a Coarse Evidence Planner, and an Evidence-Conditioned Fine Localizer. An evidence card transfers planner scores, matched cues, source-confidence proxies, modality-specific evidence, neighboring context, and a temporal prior between the latter two modules. On MedVidQA, EP-LVMQA achieves 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, improving the strongest non-ours results by 6.3 and 5.1 points. It raises Suff.@2 and Ver.@2 to 25.4 and 22.6, gains of 9.5 and 8.8 points. Under matched low-quality perturbations, average relative degradation is reduced from the strongest non-ours value of 14.6% to 11.1%. On Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights, EP-LVMQA remains broadly comparable to established task-specific localization methods.
